body:
I don't understand how the second option helps since the default is ltr and you just said that folks don't change the default.

It sounds like we want something like `default-ltr` and treat that as meaning `auto` for `title` elements?

> It sounds like we want something like `default-ltr` and treat that as meaning `auto` for `title` elements?

Something like that, I guess.

The "simplest" fix would be to add something to https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-directionality as an alternate to "If the element's dir attribute is in the auto state":

> If the element is a title element and the dir attribute is not in a defined state and the dir attribute of any ancestor elements is also not in a defined state

However, this would not help with content that might also appear in the UI, such as `<meta name=application-name value=RTLCONTENT>`, but perhaps special casing the `title` element is sufficient to deal with legacy content and we hope that new content is tagged appropriately?

@sideshowbarker it seems the validator could also help by pointing out that RTL content might not be appropriately tagged if it encounters it and doesn't see corresponding `dir` attributes and such.
Firefox used to also use first strong character before v53 (the current release).
@khaledhosny ah, if there's a related Firefox bug that would be good to list here. Do you happen to know what other browsers do?

@rniwa @rbyers who from Safari and Chrome can comment on this? In particular I'm interested in knowing whether Safari and Chrome are likely to adopt the change I propose in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2648#issuecomment-300394438.

> it seems the validator could also help by pointing out that RTL content might not be appropriately tagged if it encounters it and doesn't see corresponding `dir` attributes and such

@r12a is that a check the i18n checker also does and reports on?

@sideshowbarker i think the nearest i get to it is https://www.w3.org/International/quicktips/doc/checker.en.php#rep_markup_dir_default, which just notices a lang tag that's likely to include rtl text somewhere in the doc but discovers no dir attribute in the html tag. I raised a couple of issues at https://github.com/w3c/i18n-checker/issues to prompt me to add new tests.

fwiw, here are the tests i have for display of bidi title text in the browser chrome
https://www.w3.org/International/tests/repo/results/native-user-interfaces#windowheader
Note that i just updated the results for Firefox, which previously were the same as for Chrome/Safari - i assume that this related is what @khaledhosny just mentioned.

Regarding @upsuper 's suggestion: 

> I think there are several options:
>  -   make directionality of title element solely depend on the first strong character like what some browsers currently do, or

The problem with this is that it can break things which the content author would otherwise be able to fix. If the title is really a RTL phrase but happens to start with Latin characters (eg. CSS .... ), the first-strong approach will produce the _wrong_ direction in the tab heading. If the content author used a `dir` attribute they could fix that easily. If the `dir` attribute is no longer taken into account, they're stuck with a bad result.

> -    use the first strong character when the dir attribute of both title element and all its ancestors are in the auto state.

Did you mean, use the fs character when no dir attribute is set on the title element or its ancestors?  (If dir is not set, the direction is ltr, not auto.)

I'm not sure btw that we should extrapolate too far from testing just a few pages wrt whether people use the `dir` attribute on the `html` tag.  I see it used a lot.  (I just tried 6 arabic wikipedia pages at random and they _all_ had `dir` in the `hml` tag.)

Sometimes, however, people do put the `dir` attribute on the `body` tag, rather than on the `html` tag.  If the document is really rtl on the whole, it's waaay easier to put `dir` on the `html` tag than to include it on all the block tags, but some people simply don't realise that you can do that - i think that's a question of education, rather than something we need to bend towards.

So my main point is that by ignoring `dir` where it is used on `html` or even the `head` or `title` element tags you simply introduce other problems, and i don't think we want to go there.

The problem with using first-strong in the absence of a dir attribute is that hardly anyone uses dir="ltr" in html, precisely because it's defined as the default direction, so they haven't needed to. So by using FS we risk breaking pages that have a title such as "العربية means Arabic". Which is particularly a problem for someone creating such a page if they aren't used to the intricacies of handling rtl text.

So i'm thinking that the solution to the problem is better education, rather than changing the way the spec works. (And fixing the browsers so that they match the spec.)

> I just tried 6 arabic wikipedia pages at random and they all had dir in the hml tag

Wikipedia pages certainly all have `dir` in the `html` tag... What I tried was external pages linked from Wikipedia.

I did that again from Arabic Wikipedia, and these are the pages I checked:
* [archive.arabic.cnn.com](http://archive.arabic.cnn.com/2013/sport/10/16/intermilan.deal/) (no dir anywhere at all)
* [www.mofa.gov.sa](http://www.mofa.gov.sa/ServicesAndInformation/news/MinistryNews/Pages/ArticleID2017523132559414.aspx) (dir attribute on html)
* [ara.reuters.com](http://ara.reuters.com/article/worldNews/idARAKBN18J12K) (no dir anywhere at all)
* [www.alhayat.com](http://www.alhayat.com/Articles/22020668/%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%8A%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AA%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%B1%D9%87%D8%A7%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%B1) (CSS direction property for all elements)
* [chouftv.ma](http://chouftv.ma/press/59463-.%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8-%D9%8A%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%A8%D8%B4%D8%AF%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%AC%D9%88%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%B1%D9%87%D8%A7%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B0%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%AF%D9%81-%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%A9-%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%B1-%D9%84%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%81%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA) (CSS direction property on body)
* [mawdoo3.com](http://mawdoo3.com/%D8%B7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%82%D8%A9_%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B6%D9%8A%D8%B1_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%84%D9%88%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AA_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9) (dir attribute on html)
* [cookpad.com](https://cookpad.com/sa) (dir attribute on html)
* [www.aljazeera.net](http://www.aljazeera.net/news/arabic/2013/4/5/%d9%88%d8%ab%d8%a7%d8%a6%d9%82-%d8%aa%d9%88%d9%86%d8%b3%d9%8a%d8%a9-%d8%a8%d9%88%d8%b1%d9%82%d9%8a%d8%a8%d8%a9-%d8%ad%d8%a7%d9%88%d9%84-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a7%d9%86%d8%aa%d8%ad%d8%a7%d8%b1) (dir attribute on content elements)
* [www.turess.com](http://www.turess.com/alchourouk/3293) (CSS direction property on html and body)

So 3 in 9 actually use dir attribute on html.

(I don't understand Arabic at all. I just randomly click pages from the main page of Arabic Wikipedia, and scroll down to the external links at the end of articles and open them to check.)

> The problem with using first-strong in the absence of a dir attribute is that hardly anyone uses dir="ltr" in html, precisely because it's defined as the default direction, so they haven't needed to. So by using FS we risk breaking pages that have a title such as "العربية means Arabic". Which is particularly a problem for someone creating such a page if they aren't used to the intricacies of handling rtl text.

So the question would be, is this more common, or Arabic / Hebrew pages relying on first strong character more common? I pretty much believe it is the latter.

And also websites already depend on that most browsers using first strong character rather than the directionality. If the pages like what you mentioned is common, they are already broken, and this issue should probably have been raised long ago since browser vendors or spec should get complaint from authors of those pages. The fact that it didn't happen indicates that isn't very common, and majority of people are happy with first strong character.

@upsuper It's good for me to look at pages in the wild from time to time, so i checked out the pages you mentioned that don't use `dir` in Firefox.

    1  archive.arabic.cnn.com (no dir anywhere at all)
Uses css to set the direction of specific text blocks to rtl, which is not ideal, but there is a direction set for most of the text, at least. However no direction is set for the title element, which contains the text
ثلاثي إندونيسي يستحوذ على نادي إنتر ميلان - CNNArabic.com
which btw is therefore displayed incorrectly on FF (the CNNArabic.com should be to the left), although you can't see that on the tab because the text is too long.

    2  ara.reuters.com (no dir anywhere at all)
This page is a mess.  They try to do rtl display by using just text-align:right. Note how the sentence final periods appear at the beginning of the last line of each para, and the two quotation marks in the main title appear together.  They use margins and positioned images to make the bullets look right on the list. If a Latin text string appeared inside any sentence (which is not uncommon) the sentence would become very hard to read. They have the same issue with the title text in FF as the previous URL - the word Reuters belongs on the left of the arabic, but appears to the right. So the title display is also broken.

    3  www.alhayat.com (CSS direction property for all elements)
So actually a base direction _is_ set for the title element in this case.

    4  chouftv.ma (CSS direction property on body)
So same as the first url above.

    5 www.aljazeera.net (dir attribute on content elements)
Including `dir=rtl text-align=right` on many `p` elements, which are probably not needed, since `direction` is set on the `body` element. It, like other pages, also has multiple `meta` elements, which also don't have base direction because none is applied to contents of the `head` element.

    6 www.turess.com (CSS direction property on html and body)
So this _does_ have a base direction set for the title element.

> So 3 in 9 actually use dir attribute on html.

Taking into account that a base direction can be set using CSS (though that's not a great idea), and excluding (2), by my count, only 3 of the 9 don't have a rtl base direction set for the `title` element.

> Taking into account that a base direction can be set using CSS (though that's not a great idea), and excluding (2), by my count, only 3 of the 9 don't have a rtl base direction set for the title element.

Is it possible to make directionality depend on CSS `direction` property, then?

Also 3 of 9 is still a pretty significant percentage, and I believe you can find far fewer LTR pages which have their title start with an RTL strong character than RTL pages without base direction for title element even in your count.

> So the question would be, is this more common, or Arabic / Hebrew pages relying on first strong character more common? I pretty much believe it is the latter.
> 
> And also websites already depend on that most browsers using first strong character rather than the directionality. If the pages like what you mentioned is common, they are already broken, and this issue should probably have been raised long ago since browser vendors or spec should get complaint from authors of those pages. The fact that it didn't happen indicates that isn't very common, and majority of people are happy with first strong character.

In my experience things are not so clear cut when dealing with people who develop content in the Arabic script. We should probably ask some people who use rtl scripts before taking a decision. I've spoken with plenty who are pretty fatalistic about the fact that browsers, and many other applications, do a bad job when it comes to presenting text in their language. Even people who should know better come to just expect that it will look bad. They commonly just put up with it, or they sometimes introduce hacks that damage the data itself. But if you ask them, they are actually frustrated.
